**Coastline Freight: 60x more deploys, and the metric nobody put on the slide**

Coastline Freight moves cargo well. Its software moved slowly.

Until March 2024, the Rotterdam logistics firm shipped its dispatch platform once every eight weeks. Releases ran overnight on Saturdays, took four engineers babysitting a runbook, and roughly one in three needed a rollback by Monday morning.

"We batched everything," says Priya Raghunathan, who runs platform engineering. "Ninety changes at once. When something broke, nobody could say which one broke it."

The team moved to a continuous delivery platform that spring. The migration was not quick. Their test suite took fifty minutes and flaked often enough that engineers had learned to ignore it, so the first two months went into cutting it to nine minutes and deleting the tests nobody trusted. Only after that did automated promotion make sense.

Today Coastline deploys the dispatch service about forty times a week. Each deploy carries one merged pull request. Rollback is a button, and it gets pressed maybe twice a month without ceremony.

The numbers that changed most were not the ones the team expected. Deploy frequency went up 60x, which reads well on a slide. The figure Raghunathan cites internally is time to restore: down from eleven hours to under twenty minutes, because a broken deploy now contains one change instead of ninety.

Saturday nights are free. The four engineers who used to run releases work on routing instead.

"I would not tell anyone this fixed our culture," Raghunathan says. "It removed an excuse. We could not blame the release process anymore, so we had to look at the code."

---

Two things worth knowing before you use it: the company, quotes, and figures are invented, so they need replacing with real ones or the piece is fabricated testimony. And the shape is deliberate — the messy migration and the deflating closing quote are what keep it from reading like ad copy. If you swap those for a smooth arc, you get the genre back.
